passages.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The eyes can hold a position after a brief movement command has ended. An animal can also keep track of its location while the activity of individual neurons fluctuates. [Both abilities require a useful quantity to remain represented in a changing biological system.]{.key-statement} The three papers study different parts of this problem: the loss of a stored value, the origin of slow eye motion, and the arrangement of spatial firing patterns. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

Before asking how a circuit keeps a value, we need to know what its signals do. We begin with brief neural spikes and the eye muscles they activate, explaining how repeated activation can maintain an eye angle. We next establish the equations that connect spikes, synaptic input and firing rate. With that physical meaning in place, we ask how a pattern of rates represents an angle or an animal's location. A model of spike counts shows why one brief observation can be uncertain and how combining counts from several cells can help. We then follow these ingredients through the 2012 network simulation: what the computer updates, how the cells interact, and what the comparison with theory establishes. Finally, we separate shared variation, random spreading and a change in the average value. These distinctions prepare us to interpret both a memory model and measurements of eye motion.
For the eye to stay directed at a target, its muscles must keep exerting force after the movement command ends.

<!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = NO --> [A neuron communicates through brief electrical events called [**spike**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s.]{.definition-explanation} [A [**firing rate**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the expected number of spikes per unit time.]{.definition-explanation} A rate of 20 hertz means an average of 20 spikes per second under the specified conditions, rather than a promise of one spike every 50 milliseconds. <!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = YES -->

**Anatomy: muscles turn the eyeball.** In humans and macaques, the eyeball rotates within the bony eye socket, or orbit. [The six [**extraocular muscles**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} attach to the outside of the eyeball and control its orientation.]{.definition-explanation} The medial rectus pulls it toward the nose; the lateral rectus pulls it away. The superior and inferior rectus and the two oblique muscles contribute to vertical movement and rotation about the line of sight. Their actions depend on the eye's orientation.[^p-eye-anatomy]

[**Ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [are neurons that activate these muscles through long nerve fibres.]{.definition-explanation} Their cell bodies lie in brainstem groups, and these fibres travel through three cranial nerves. The abducens nerve, VI, supplies the lateral rectus; the trochlear nerve, IV, supplies the superior oblique; the oculomotor nerve, III, supplies the other four. For horizontal gaze, changing the relative pull of the medial and lateral rectus rotates the eye. [A force's turning effect is its [**torque**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Opposing torques can balance even while the muscles remain under tension.[^p-eye-anatomy]

**Repeated spikes maintain tension.** Each motor spike affects muscle force for longer than the electrical event lasts. Repeated activation and the combined action of many muscle fibres give a smoother force than a sequence of isolated eye movements. [**Tonic firing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [means sustained firing during the holding period.]{.definition-explanation} It need not be perfectly periodic. During a rapid repositioning movement, called a [**saccade**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a brief strong drive moves the eye; a sustained position-dependent drive then holds the new angle. This is the pulse-and-step description: the step means continuing drive, not one more spike.[^p-eye-mechanics][^p-eye-plasticity]
The mechanical properties contribute in different ways:

[**Elasticity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [creates restoring forces when muscles and surrounding tissues are stretched.]{.definition-explanation} At an off-centre gaze angle, active muscle torque must balance the restoring tendency.

[**Viscosity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [resists motion and dissipates mechanical energy.]{.definition-explanation} It damps rapid changes but supplies no holding torque once velocity is zero.

[**Inertia**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [is resistance to a change in angular velocity.]{.definition-explanation} It matters during acceleration, not as a force holding a stationary eye. In primate eye movements, elastic and viscous effects dominate inertia.[^p-eye-mechanics]

[Mechanical damping smooths movement; sustained neural drive selects the angle around which the eye is held. Inertia cannot preserve a stationary gaze against an unbalanced elastic pull.]{.key-statement}
So far we have followed the output from motor neurons to muscles. The next step is a model of how neurons act on one another and sustain a signal.

**Neural mechanism.** How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of a spike? In this model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually. [Incoming activations determine new firing rates. The resulting spikes renew those activations. This feedback can support activity after the external stimulus has ended.]{.key-statement}

[Neurons affect one another through connections called [**synapse**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s.]{.definition-explanation} In the models used here, inputs have two contrasting effects:
[An [**excitatory input**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} increases a receiving neuron's tendency to fire.]{.definition-explanation}
[An [**inhibitory input**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} reduces it.]{.definition-explanation}

The effect of a spike can last beyond the spike itself because synaptic input decays over time. [When neurons send signals back into the same population, the circuit has [**recurrent connectivity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Such feedback can maintain activity after an external signal disappears.

Burak and Fiete (2012) use the following equations for interactions inside a neural circuit. These describe synaptic activity; muscle motion is a later part of the pathway. The model assumes fixed connection weights, constant input biases and a common synaptic decay time. Its statistical rule for spike timing is explained in the [spike-count section](#sec-foundations-poisson).[^p1-model]

**Model dynamics: Burak and Fiete (2012), Equation 7.** [The [**synaptic activation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $s_i$ tracks the decaying effect of neuron $i$'s outgoing spikes on receiving cells.]{.definition-explanation} The dot means $\dot s_i=ds_i/dt$, and $\tau$ is the decay time in seconds. The index $\alpha$ numbers the spikes of neuron $i$, with spike $\alpha$ occurring at time $t_i^\alpha$. [The [**Dirac delta**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $\delta(t-t_i^\alpha)$ represents an instantaneous unit pulse at that spike time; its integral across that time is one.]{.definition-explanation} The paper writes the activation dynamics as

Between spikes, the right-hand side is zero and activation decays. Integrating through one spike gives a one-unit increase in $s_i$. [Read Eq. 7 as a balance: spikes add activation, while the term $s_i/\tau$ removes it.]{.key-statement} [Original Eq. 7, PDF p. 5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=5).
**Equivalent count form.** Let $N_i(t)$ count neuron $i$'s spikes up to time $t$. Integrating the pulse train counts the spikes, so the same dynamics can be written as
Equivalently, if its spikes occur at times $t_i^\alpha$,

once the contribution from any activation present at the starting time has decayed. The sum includes a spike at time $t$, so it gives the activation immediately after that spike. Here $s_i$ is dimensionless in the convention that each spike adds one unit.
For five illustrative spike times, the plot shows the events and the activation they leave behind.

**From activation to new spikes: Equations 8 and 9.** The total input $g_i$ to neuron $i$ combines the activation arriving from other cells with a constant input bias $b_i$. The fixed connection weight $W_{ij}$ says how the activation of neuron $j$ affects the input to neuron $i$:

[The [**neural transfer function**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $\phi$ converts total input into a nonnegative firing rate $r_i$, in spikes per second.]{.definition-explanation} Thus
These equations specify how the input sets the rate; they do not prescribe each spike's time.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> For example, increasing input might increase firing linearly over some input range, or exponentially. The paper allows general connectivity and transfer functions at first ([Model, Eqs. 7–9, p. 5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=5&zoom=125,0,372)).[^p1-model] <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> A spike from cell $j$ raises $s_j$ by one and therefore changes the input to cell $i$ by $W_{ij}$. That contribution then decays over time $\tau$. For an increasing transfer function, a positive weight raises the receiving cell's rate and a negative weight lowers it. The resulting new spikes affect other cells in turn. Thus the weights set where a disturbance goes, the transfer function sets the rate response, and $\tau$ sets how long each synaptic contribution lasts. The input $g_i$ is in the model's input units. It is not specified as a measured membrane voltage. <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

Together, Eqs. 7–9 describe one feedback cycle: spikes change synaptic activation, weighted activation changes input, and input changes the rate of new spikes. The next question is how the resulting pattern of rates can represent an eye angle or location.

[A [**tuning curve**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} gives a neuron's expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable.]{.definition-explanation} For eye angle $\theta$, a simple local model is $r_i(\theta)=r_{i,0}+k_i\theta$. Neuron $i$ has baseline rate $r_{i,0}$ in spikes per second and slope $k_i$ in spikes per second per degree. This rate baseline is different from the input bias $b_i$ in Eq. 8. The linear expression can describe an active range, but it must be modified where it would predict negative firing. The eye paper includes a firing threshold and terms for movement as well as position.[^f-eye]
Different cells have different tuning curves. The vector

<!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeCarries = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = NO --> [is a [**population code**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: the pattern across $N$ neurons carries information about $\theta$.]{.definition-explanation} The position of a cell in this vector is a neuron identity, rather than a location in physical space. [Reading a value from observed spikes is [**decoding**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} [Establishing a population pattern from an input is [**encoding**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} [The 2012 paper asks how accurately the network can maintain such a pattern using its own noisy activity.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeCarries = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> Spatial tuning gives a second example. In the hippocampus, a brain structure involved in memory and navigation, a place cell fires strongly in one or more localized regions of an environment. A connected region of elevated spatial firing is a place field. One neuron can have several fields. [A [**rate map**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} estimates the rate at each position by dividing the spikes recorded there by the time spent there.]{.definition-explanation} Sparse visits, smoothing, and firing cutoffs therefore affect the estimated map and its fields. A field in a model's expected rate and a field extracted from finite recordings are related objects with different measurement uncertainties.[^f-place] <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->
The hippocampal areas CA3 and CA1 contain place cells, but their connections differ:
CA3 supplies major input to CA1 and has substantial recurrent excitation.
CA1 also receives input from entorhinal cortex and has much less local recurrent excitation.

[A [**grid cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, found in entorhinal cortex, has repeated spatial fields that often form an approximately hexagonal pattern in a two-dimensional arena.]{.definition-explanation} These repeated grid fields and a place cell's irregular multiple fields should be kept distinct. A model explaining CA1's output maps need not identify where the animal's position estimate is maintained.[^f-anatomy]

A tuning curve describes expected activity, but a brief spike observation can differ each time the same value is represented. [The 2012 model describes this variability with a [**Poisson process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Take $n$ large enough that $p<1$. This construction assumes a constant chance of a spike per unit time and independence between nonoverlapping bins. In the continuous-time limit, the chance of two or more spikes in one bin becomes negligible compared with its width. These are assumptions of the Poisson model, not properties of every recorded neuron.[^f-poisson-limit]

The factor $\lambda^k$ comes from the $k$ spike probabilities together with the number of possible bin locations, and $k!$ corrects repeated counting.]{.key-statement} In particular, $e^{-\lambda}$ is the probability of no spikes. A positive expected count can therefore coexist with a silent observation.

This is why collecting more independent spikes can improve a rate estimate. It also means that increasing a firing-rate scale does not keep absolute noise amplitude fixed. Comparisons between networks must specify which quantities are held constant.[^f-poisson] <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

In a recurrent network, however, $r(t)$ itself depends on earlier spikes. The whole-interval count need not then be Poisson. The useful independence statement is local and conditional: given the current modeled state, the elementary spike-generation noise is independent across cells in the basic 2012 model. The changing state can still produce correlations across time and across neurons. [The [**coefficient of variation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, or CV, of interspike intervals, the times between successive spikes, is their standard deviation divided by their mean.]{.definition-explanation} A homogeneous Poisson process has exponential intervals and CV equal to one. More regular firing can have CV below one, as in the ocular motor neurons analyzed in 2022.
[The count variance divided by mean count is the [**Fano factor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}]{.definition-explanation}. Its value also depends on the counting interval.
CV and Fano factor cannot be substituted for one another without additional assumptions.

Can a network keep firing while losing the value it represents? Burak and Fiete (2012) test this by following the spikes and synaptic activations generated by Eqs. 7–9. These simulations support the paper's central theory of memory error: they test whether the directly simulated spikes produce the predicted changes in the stored value.[^f-network-simulation]

**The simulated system.** The computer stores one changing activation $s_i$ for each neuron. It calculates each input $g_i$ and rate $r_i$ from the current activations. The connections $W_{ij}$, input biases $b_i$, decay time $\tau$ and transfer function $\phi$ stay fixed during a run. Constant bias remains present, but no continuing stimulus fixes the remembered value. The model follows recurrent neural activity; it does not calculate muscle forces, membrane-voltage waveforms or learning of connections.

In the ring example, 1,024 neurons are ordered by their [**preferred angle**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, [the represented angle at which each neuron's expected firing rate is highest.]{.definition-explanation} [An [**activity bump**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a localized peak of firing rates across these neurons; its position represents the stored angle.]{.definition-explanation} The ring describes the ordering of preferred angles, not an anatomical circle of cells. The published connections are inhibitory and depend on angular separation. Nearby preferred angles have weak mutual inhibition, while the active group suppresses competing activity farther away. The chosen connection profile and firing rule sustain a localized pattern. Random spike timing can move its peak even while the pattern persists.

**How neurons depend on one another.** A spike in cell $j$ increases $s_j$ by one. Every receiving cell $i$ then gets an input change $W_{ij}$, which changes its rate through $\phi$. Its later spikes feed back into the network. [Independent random spike draws at given rates do not make the neurons' activity independent: earlier spikes change the rates used for later draws.]{.key-statement}
For the ring simulation, one step of duration $h$ follows this cycle:
Calculate $g_i$ and $r_i$ from all current activations.
Draw a spike indicator $X_i$: it is one with probability $r_i h$ and zero otherwise, independently across cells conditional on those current rates.
Reduce the old activation by its decay over the step and add the generated spike:

The next step uses these updated activations. This [**Euler update**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [approximates continuous decay by the current rate of change times the step duration.]{.definition-explanation} The one-spike draw requires $r_i h$ to be small. The authors use $h=0.1$ ms and $\tau=10$ ms. Their two-population example requires a spike-count rule suitable for aggregate population activity; the one-spike restriction above belongs to the ring implementation. The [simulation chapter](ch-simulating-memory.html#sec-simulating-memory-state) gives the full settings and numerical cautions.

Before comparing simulated motion with theory, we need a measure of how far the represented value moves. Let $x(t)$ be that value at absolute time $t$, and let $\ell$ be the time between two observations, called the lag. [The [**displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $\Delta x=x(t+\ell)-x(t)$.]{.definition-explanation} The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the average of $(\Delta x)^2$ over intervals with the same lag. The average can use different starting times along a recording, repeated trials, or both; which intervals can be combined depends on whether their movement statistics are comparable. Squaring prevents leftward and rightward changes from cancelling.

For an angle measured in degrees, MSD has units degrees squared. An MSD plot puts lag on the horizontal axis and MSD on the vertical axis. Lag is a duration, not the clock time at which an interval starts. If the statistics change during a trial, the MSD can depend on that starting time as well as on lag.

[A straight MSD curve on ordinary axes means that the average squared displacement grows at a constant rate over that range.]{.key-statement} The zero-mean diffusion model taught in the next chapter gives $\operatorname{MSD}(\ell)=2D\ell$, where the diffusion coefficient $D$ is half the rate of displacement-variance growth. The MSD slope is $2D$ in degrees squared per second. On axes that plot logarithms, a relation $\operatorname{MSD}\propto\ell^\beta$ has slope $\beta$: diffusion has slope one, while constant-velocity motion has slope two. A slope alone does not identify the neural cause. Bias, smoothing by muscles, boundaries and the range of lags measured can change the curve.

**What is measured and compared.** At each step, the ring's angle is read from the preferred angle of the neuron with the highest instantaneous rate. The authors measure how much that angle changes over different time intervals and average the squared changes. They independently calculate the predicted spreading from the same network's steady activity in the absence of noise. In [Figure 2C–D](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=3), simulation points agree with these theoretical curves without fitting a free diffusion parameter. Over short intervals, the mean squared change grows approximately linearly with elapsed time. Over long intervals, wrapping angle differences into a single turn limits the plotted error. That flattening does not mean the original angle has been recovered.

[Figure 2E–G](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=3) repeats the test with two mutually inhibiting units, which can represent two groups of neurons. Their difference in firing rates represents the stored value. Agreement in this second design checks that the prediction is not specific to the ring's symmetry.

**Relation to biological data.** [Figure 2 compares theory with simulated data. It does not fit the memory errors of a recorded animal.]{.key-statement} The paper motivates persistent activity and variable spiking using earlier experiments, and proposes tests using measured tuning curves. It also notes that eye-position neurons can spike more regularly than a Poisson process, so the Poisson formula cannot be applied directly to those recordings. The [2022 eye-drift study](ch-eye-drift.html) supplies a separate comparison with recorded neural activity and eye motion. Here the established result is narrower: the specified interacting network models produce the memory spreading predicted by the theory.[^f-network-data]
The next section explains how measured changes can distinguish shared neural variation from a directional bias when the output is an eye movement.

During fixation, a monkey tries to keep looking at a stationary target, yet its eye moves slightly. A changing command from the brain can make many motor neurons change their firing together. Their spikes act on the eye muscles, which turn the eye. An individual motor neuron also adds spike variability of its own. The 2022 paper asks how much of the observed movement follows a shared neural command, and whether that command itself wanders over time.[^f-eye]

<!-- vale ai-tells.NegatedSubject = NO --> [Covariance asks which recorded changes occur together. Displacement statistics ask how far the eye moves and how that movement grows with elapsed time.]{.key-statement} Neither measurement by itself identifies the neural circuit responsible. <!-- vale ai-tells.NegatedSubject = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = NO --> **Physical meaning: a shared command can survive averaging across neurons.** If a common input raises the firing of many motor neurons that pull the eye in the same direction, their effects add. Independent extra and missing spikes partly cancel when those neurons act together. The paper compares the measured eye displacement with a displacement predicted from one neuron's spikes, after converting both to degrees. That prediction is an analysis of a recording, not an extra command sent to the muscles. A relationship between the two is evidence to test against a model of shared input and private noise. It does not mean that the one recorded cell causes all the movement. <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = YES -->

[**Covariance**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [measures whether two signals tend to be above their own averages together or on opposite sides of those averages.]{.definition-explanation} Positive covariance between the two displacements means that above-average changes in the neural prediction tend to accompany above-average changes in eye position. [The [**correlation coefficient**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, written $\rho$, expresses this shared variation relative to the spread of each signal.]{.definition-explanation} Extra private noise can lower $\rho$ even when the shared drive has not weakened. The [eye-drift calculation](ch-eye-drift.html#sec-eye-chi) explains why a modest correlation need not mean a small shared contribution to movement.
Let $X$ and $Y$ be the two displacements, in degrees, across repeated intervals of the same duration. Subtracting each average leaves its fluctuation. Their covariance is
Here it has units degrees squared. In general its units are the product of the two signals' units. Variance is $\operatorname{Cov}(X,X)$. Expanding the square of a centered sum or difference gives
For nonzero variances, correlation is

<!-- vale ai-tells.NegatedObject = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> It is dimensionless and lies between $-1$ and $1$. Independence gives zero covariance when these moments exist. Zero covariance alone does not imply independence. <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.NegatedObject = YES -->

To see the physical roles, write $X=g_X S+\epsilon_X$ and $Y=g_Y S+\epsilon_Y$. Here $S$ is a shared displacement signal in degrees, the dimensionless [**gain**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s $g_X,g_Y$ multiply its contribution in each recording, and $\epsilon_X,\epsilon_Y$ are private contributions in degrees. If all three random contributions are independent,

Increasing private variance increases the denominator of $\rho$ without increasing the covariance. Changing a gain changes the measured covariance even if the shared source is unchanged. This simple construction explains the need for calibration and explicit noise assumptions. It is not the paper's full inference model.

**Physical meaning: random wandering differs from a persistent directional error.** Apply the displacement measure above to horizontal eye angle $x(t)$ in degrees, using a lag $\ell$ in seconds. A random change in the maintained command can move the eye left in one interval and right in another. The average displacement can then be close to zero while individual displacements are large. A persistent imbalance in the command can instead make the average displacement grow in one direction.
